referents.label: LUCA, the Last Universal Common Ancestor
The Change in Volcanic Volatile Composition

claims.statement: Lead isotopes in meteorites and in ocean sediment converge on an Earth about 4.55 billion years old.
claims.asserted_by: Patterson 1956, Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta

status_timeline.source: Patterson 1956, Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta — first isochron age for Earth and meteorites together, 4.55 ± 0.07 Ga
radiometric consensus, 1970s — independent chronometers repeatedly reproduce ~4.55 Ga; no serious rival has ever emerged

claims.statement: Hafnium-tungsten dating puts the end of Earth's main accretion some tens of millions of years after the Sun.
claims.asserted_by: Hf–W isotope chronology, diffuse consensus 2000s–2010s (no single originating paper)

status_timeline.source: Hf–W core-formation chronometry, early 2000s — deliberately vague; the result emerged across several groups, not one paper
cosmochemical debate, 2010s — everyone agrees accretion closed after the Sun, but the 30–100 Myr window is still argued and the model ages depend on assumed impactor cores

claims.statement: The Moon condensed from debris blasted into orbit when a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth off-centre.
claims.asserted_by: Hartmann & Davis 1975, Icarus

status_timeline.source: Hartmann & Davis 1975, Icarus — satellite-sized planetesimals proposed as the Moon's source; Cameron & Ward reach the same idea independently at LPSC in 1976
Conference on the Origin of the Moon, Kona 1984 — giant impact wins the field largely by elimination of fission, capture and co-accretion, but without simulations
Canup & Asphaug 2001, Nature — hydrodynamic simulations finally reproduce the Moon's mass, iron deficit and angular momentum

claims.statement: Simulations show an impactor near a tenth of Earth's mass gives the right mass, spin and iron budget for the Moon.
claims.asserted_by: Canup & Asphaug 2001, Nature

status_timeline.source: Canup & Asphaug 2001, Nature — the canonical low-velocity, grazing giant impact
isotopic-crisis literature, early 2010s — the canonical impact makes a Moon built mostly of Theia, contradicting identical O and Ti isotopes

claims.statement: Uranium-lead and hafnium ages on Apollo 14 zircons date the Moon to 4.51 Ga, within 60 Myr of the Sun.
claims.asserted_by: Barboni et al. 2017, Science Advances

status_timeline.source: Barboni et al. 2017, Science Advances 3:e1602365 — concordant U–Pb ages on eight Apollo 14 zircon fragments, with Hf model ages in support
lunar chronology debate, ~2020 — a 4.51 Ga Moon conflicts with the Hf–W model ages that favour a later impact, and eight grains is a thin sample

claims.statement: Tungsten model ages push the giant impact later, nearer 4.45 Ga, roughly 100 Myr after the solar system began.
claims.asserted_by: Hf–W lunar model-age literature, 2000s–2010s (diffuse; deliberately not pinned to one paper)

status_timeline.source: Hf–W lunar chronometry, mid-2000s — vague by design; several groups report ages in the 4.42–4.48 Ga range
cosmochemical reviews, early 2010s — a giant impact more than 50 Myr after CAI formation became the majority textbook position, though never unanimous

claims.statement: Apollo highland rocks cluster near 3.9 Ga, read as a brief cataclysmic spike of impacts on Moon and Earth.
claims.asserted_by: Tera, Papanastassiou & Wasserburg 1974, Earth and Planetary Science Letters

status_timeline.source: Tera, Papanastassiou & Wasserburg 1974, EPSL — isotopic evidence for a terminal lunar cataclysm
Gomes, Levison, Tsiganis & Morbidelli 2005, Nature — the Nice model supplies a dynamical cause and the LHB becomes textbook
Boehnke & Harrison 2016, PNAS — the age cluster may be a sampling artifact, not an impact spike

claims.statement: The 3.9 Ga age cluster may be an artifact of sampling Imbrium ejecta rather than a real bombardment spike.
claims.asserted_by: Boehnke & Harrison 2016, PNAS

status_timeline.source: Boehnke & Harrison 2016, PNAS — 'Illusory late heavy bombardments'; a monotonic decline reproduces the same age histogram
sample-bias literature, late 2010s — several groups agree the cataclysm is unproven; a milder declining flux is now widely preferred

claims.statement: Migration of Jupiter and Saturn through a resonance destabilised the outer belt and rained debris on the inner planets.
claims.asserted_by: Gomes, Levison, Tsiganis & Morbidelli 2005, Nature

status_timeline.source: Gomes, Levison, Tsiganis & Morbidelli 2005, Nature — planetary migration as the trigger for a cataclysmic bombardment
Boehnke & Harrison 2016, PNAS — if there was no spike, the model explains something that never happened

Nesvorný, Vokrouhlický, Bottke & Levison 2018, Nature Astronomy 2:878–882, doi 10.1038/s41550-018-0564-3 — the fragile Patroclus–Menoetius binary Jupiter Trojan only survives capture if the planetesimal disk was dispersed within ~100 Myr of Solar System birth. That moves the instability roughly 600 Myr earlier than the Late Heavy Bombardment it was proposed to explain, so migration can no longer be its trigger even if the bombardment itself is real.

claims.statement: Ocean-boiling impacts could have repeatedly sterilised the surface, delaying or resetting the start of life.
claims.asserted_by: Maher & Stevenson 1988, Nature

status_timeline.source: Maher & Stevenson 1988, Nature 331:612 — 'Impact frustration of the origin of life'; abiogenesis possible by 4.0–4.2 Ga if life started at deep vents
Boehnke & Harrison 2016, PNAS — with no cataclysm, the sterilisation window largely dissolves

claims.statement: A 4.404-billion-year-old Jack Hills zircon carries oxygen isotopes implying crust already altered by liquid water.
claims.asserted_by: Wilde, Valley, Peck & Graham 2001, Nature

status_timeline.source: Wilde, Valley, Peck & Graham 2001, Nature — oldest known terrestrial mineral; a cool, wet Hadean
Hadean zircon debate, mid-2000s — critics argued the heavy δ18O could reflect later alteration or radiogenic Pb mobility
Valley et al. 2014, Nature Geoscience — atom-probe tomography confirms the age and closes the main objection

claims.statement: Atom-probe imaging of lead clusters inside the grain shows the Hadean age is real, not a disturbed artifact.
claims.asserted_by: Valley et al. 2014, Nature Geoscience

status_timeline.source: Valley et al. 2014, Nature Geoscience — nanoscale Pb clustering dated at 3.4 Ga, leaving the 4.4 Ga crystallisation intact
Hadean geochronology consensus, late 2010s — the 4.4 Ga Jack Hills age is no longer seriously disputed

claims.statement: A liquid hydrosphere by 4.4 Ga removes the main obstacle to life having started in the Hadean.
claims.asserted_by: Bell, Boehnke, Harrison & Mao 2015, PNAS

status_timeline.source: Bell, Boehnke, Harrison & Mao 2015, PNAS — a habitable Hadean surface argued from zircon evidence
Hadean habitability literature, ~2020 — the 'cool early Earth' is broadly accepted even by those who reject Hadean life

claims.statement: Carbon-rich filaments in the 3.465-billion-year-old Apex chert were described as cyanobacteria-like microfossils.
claims.asserted_by: Schopf 1993, Science

status_timeline.source: Schopf 1993, Science — eleven taxa of filamentous microfossils from the Apex chert, Pilbara
palaeontological textbook consensus, mid-1990s — the Apex filaments become the standard 'oldest fossils' in teaching and museums
Brasier et al. 2002, Nature — the filaments reinterpreted as abiogenic graphite in a hydrothermal vein
Schopf, Kitajima, Spicuzza, Kudryavtsev & Valley 2018, PNAS 115:53 — SIMS δ13C of −31 to −39‰ tracks morphospecies; the authors call biogenicity confirmed, sceptics are unmoved

claims.statement: The Apex 'microfossils' are more likely abiogenic graphite artifacts from a hot-spring vein, not fossil cells.
claims.asserted_by: Brasier et al. 2002, Nature

status_timeline.source: Brasier et al. 2002, Nature — 'Questioning the evidence for Earth's oldest fossils'
biogenicity debate, ~2010s — neither side concedes; the Apex case becomes the standard cautionary tale for biosignatures

claims.statement: A 3.43-billion-year-old reef of layered stromatolites in the Pilbara gives ecosystem-scale evidence of early life.
claims.asserted_by: Allwood, Walter, Kamber, Marshall & Burch 2006, Nature

status_timeline.source: Allwood et al. 2006, Nature — Strelley Pool Chert stromatolite reef; morphological variety argues against an abiotic origin
Allwood et al. 2009, PNAS — environmental controls on stromatolite form; now the most widely accepted Archean biosignature

claims.statement: Cone-shaped layered structures in 3.7-billion-year-old Greenland rocks were read as the oldest stromatolites.
claims.asserted_by: Nutman, Bennett, Friend, Van Kranendonk & Chivas 2016, Nature

status_timeline.source: Nutman et al. 2016, Nature — 3,700 Myr-old stromatolites newly exposed by snowmelt at Isua
Allwood et al. 2018, Nature — independent analysis finds deformation structures, no biological signal

Nutman, Bennett, Friend & Van Kranendonk 2021, Earth and Planetary Science Letters 562:116850 — 'In support of rare relict ~3700 Ma stromatolites'; argues the tested outcrop was atypically deformed. Unresolved.

claims.statement: Re-examined in three dimensions, the Isua cones are deformation ridges whose chemistry carries no biological signal.
claims.asserted_by: Allwood, Rosing, Flannery, Hurowitz & Heirwegh 2018, Nature

status_timeline.source: Allwood et al. 2018, Nature — 'Reassessing evidence of life in 3,700-million-year-old rocks of Greenland'
Nutman et al. 2021, Earth and Planetary Science Letters 562:116850 — reply in support of the relict stromatolites; the community remains divided

claims.statement: Haematite tubes in Quebec vent rocks, at least 3.77 and perhaps 4.28 Ga old, are read as fossil vent microbes.
claims.asserted_by: Dodd et al. 2017, Nature

status_timeline.source: Dodd et al. 2017, Nature — micrometre haematite filaments in Nuvvuagittuq banded iron formation
biosignature-scepticism literature, late 2010s — abiotic haematite filaments are known, and the host rock's age itself spans 3.77–4.28 Ga

claims.statement: Graphite sealed inside a 4.1-billion-year-old zircon carries a light carbon signature that could be biological.
claims.asserted_by: Bell, Boehnke, Harrison & Mao 2015, PNAS

status_timeline.source: Bell, Boehnke, Harrison & Mao 2015, PNAS — one graphite-bearing grain out of 10,000; δ13C of −24‰, framed only as 'potentially biogenic'
isotope-scepticism literature, late 2010s — abiotic carbon can reach −24‰; a single grain cannot carry the claim. Never consensus.

claims.statement: Ribosomal RNA from every cell traces back to one shared ancestral population, split into three primary lineages.
claims.asserted_by: Woese & Fox 1977, PNAS

status_timeline.source: Woese & Fox 1977, PNAS — the primary kingdoms; a universal molecular tree with a single root
microbiological resistance, ~1980 — the archaeal domain and the single-ancestor rooting were both widely rejected at first
genomic-era consensus, mid-1990s — whole-genome sequencing vindicates the three-domain rRNA tree and a universal ancestor

claims.statement: LUCA must predate the oldest accepted biosignatures, so it lived no later than about 3.5 billion years ago.
claims.asserted_by: geobiological consensus since the late 20th century; no single originating paper (a floor set by the Archean rock record, not a measurement)

status_timeline.source: early Precambrian palaeobiology, ~1980 — honest vagueness: the minimum-age argument accreted across many authors as Archean microfossils accumulated
geobiological consensus, ~2000 — that LUCA is older than the oldest credible biosignature is the one LUCA date nobody disputes; it is also the least informative

claims.statement: Molecular clocks on gene families that duplicated before LUCA place it around 4.2 billion years ago.
claims.asserted_by: Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution

status_timeline.source: Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution — calibrated clocks on pre-LUCA gene duplicates give 4.09–4.33 Ga

claims.statement: Older molecular-clock studies spread LUCA anywhere from 3.5 to 4.5 Ga, a band wider than most fossil disputes.
claims.asserted_by: molecular-clock literature, 1990s–2010s (deliberately vague; the estimates never converged)

status_timeline.source: early universal molecular clocks, 1990s — honest vagueness: dozens of incompatible estimates, no single canonical paper
Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution — a properly calibrated relaxed clock narrows the range considerably

claims.statement: LUCA looks like an anaerobic, hydrogen-using autotroph at home in a hydrothermal vent, not a generalist.
claims.asserted_by: Weiss et al. 2016, Nature Microbiology

status_timeline.source: Weiss et al. 2016, Nature Microbiology 1:16116 — 355 protein families reconstruct a thermophilic, H2-dependent, N2-fixing LUCA
Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution — reconstructs a far larger LUCA of ~2,600 proteins, a complex acetogen inside an existing ecosystem

claims.statement: Life's origin preceded LUCA by an unknown span: LUCA was already a complex cell embedded in an ecosystem.
claims.asserted_by: Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution

status_timeline.source: Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution — LUCA's inferred metabolism implies recycling partners, so it was not the first cell

claims.statement: Steranes and 2-methylhopanes in 2.7-billion-year-old Pilbara shales were taken as cyanobacterial and eukaryote traces.
claims.asserted_by: Brocks, Logan, Buick & Summons 1999, Science

status_timeline.source: Brocks, Logan, Buick & Summons 1999, Science — Archean molecular fossils push oxygenic photosynthesis back 300 Myr before the GOE
biomarker consensus, early 2000s — the 2.7 Ga 'whiff of oxygen' becomes a standard fixture of early-Earth reviews
Rasmussen, Fletcher, Brocks & Kilburn 2008, Nature — the biomarkers are younger contaminants, not indigenous

claims.statement: The Archean biomarkers are younger contaminants: their carbon isotopes clash with the kerogen they sit in.
claims.asserted_by: Rasmussen, Fletcher, Brocks & Kilburn 2008, Nature

status_timeline.source: Rasmussen et al. 2008, Nature — carbon isotopes of the hydrocarbons clash with coexisting kerogen
French et al. 2015, PNAS — ultraclean redrilling of the same rocks finds no syngenetic steranes; Brocks is a co-author on the reappraisal

claims.statement: Molybdenum isotopes in 2.95-billion-year-old South African shales imply oxygen production long before the GOE.
claims.asserted_by: Planavsky et al. 2014, Nature Geoscience

status_timeline.source: Planavsky et al. 2014, Nature Geoscience 7:283 — Mo and Fe isotopes in the Pongola Supergroup imply oxygen oases half a billion years before the GOE
oxygen-oasis debate, late 2010s — the Mo signal is small and Mn-oxidation alternatives are argued; a genuine live dispute, not a settled result

claims.statement: Oxygenic photosynthesis may have evolved only shortly before 2.4 Ga, with oxygen then accumulating almost at once.
claims.asserted_by: Kopp, Kirschvink, Hilburn & Nash 2005, PNAS

status_timeline.source: Kopp, Kirschvink, Hilburn & Nash 2005, PNAS — cyanobacteria radiate just before the Makganyene snowball, not hundreds of Myr earlier
oxygenation debate, 2010s — trace-metal and Mn-oxidation proxies still argue for oxygenic photosynthesis well before 2.5 Ga

claims.statement: Whenever it began, oxygenic photosynthesis was certainly running by 2.4 Ga: nothing else oxygenates a planet.
claims.asserted_by: geobiological consensus, 2000s–2010s; no single originating paper (an inference from the Great Oxidation Event itself, not a direct date)

status_timeline.source: early-Earth reviews, mid-2000s — deliberately vague: the floor follows from the GOE and is stated in passing by almost everyone
Lyons, Reinhard & Planavsky 2014, Nature — reviews treat a pre-GOE origin of oxygenic photosynthesis as given; only the size of the lead time is argued

claims.statement: Cyanobacterial oxygen destroyed the methane greenhouse and pushed free oxygen permanently into the air.
claims.asserted_by: Kopp, Kirschvink, Hilburn & Nash 2005, PNAS

status_timeline.source: Kopp et al. 2005, PNAS — oxygen as a planetary poison that could flip climate in as little as 1 Myr
Lyons, Reinhard & Planavsky 2014, Nature — biological oxygen production as the driver of the GOE is not seriously disputed

claims.statement: Atmospheric oxygen first rose between 2.45 and 2.32 billion years ago, bracketed by South African and Canadian strata.
claims.asserted_by: Bekker et al. 2004, Nature

status_timeline.source: Bekker et al. 2004, Nature 427:117 — 'Dating the rise of atmospheric oxygen' pins the transition in the Transvaal and Huronian successions
Lyons, Reinhard & Planavsky 2014, Nature — the 2.45–2.32 Ga window is the standard GOE onset interval and remains so

claims.statement: Mass-independent sulfur fractionation disappears after ~2.4 Ga, the sharpest fingerprint of an oxygenating sky.
claims.asserted_by: Farquhar, Bao & Thiemens 2000, Science

status_timeline.source: Farquhar, Bao & Thiemens 2000, Science 289:756 — anomalous S-33 in Archean sulfides requires an ozone-free, oxygen-free atmosphere
Pavlov & Kasting 2002, Astrobiology 2:27 — photochemical modelling ties the signal to oxygen below 1e-5 PAL; now the GOE's smoking gun

claims.statement: Oxygen did not simply stay up: permanent atmospheric oxygenation was delayed by ~200 Myr, to about 2.22 Ga.
claims.asserted_by: Poulton et al. 2021, Nature

status_timeline.source: Poulton et al. 2021, Nature 592:232 — Transvaal drill core shows the MIF signal returning repeatedly after 2.45 Ga; permanence arrives with the Lomagundi excursion
oxygenation-timing literature, 2020s — a stepped, oscillating GOE is gaining ground but the endpoint is still argued

claims.statement: Free oxygen made sterol synthesis and aerobic respiration possible, opening the way to the eukaryotic cell.
claims.asserted_by: geobiological consensus since the 1970s; no single originating paper (sterol biosynthesis requires molecular oxygen)

status_timeline.source: early geobiology, ~1970 — honest vagueness: the oxygen-prerequisite argument accreted across many authors rather than one paper
geobiological consensus, ~2000 — the oxygen threshold for eukaryotes is standard, though the causal tightness is still argued
eukaryogenesis debate, late 2010s — anaerobic Asgard-archaea models make oxygen a permission rather than a trigger

claims.statement: As oxygen rose the methane greenhouse collapsed, plunging Earth into the Paleoproterozoic Makganyene snowball at ~2.3 Ga.
claims.asserted_by: Kopp, Kirschvink, Hilburn & Nash 2005, PNAS

status_timeline.source: Kopp et al. 2005, PNAS — the Paleoproterozoic snowball as a climate disaster caused by life itself; note this is 1.6 Gyr before the Cryogenian snowballs
Paleoproterozoic glaciation literature, 2010s — the methane-collapse mechanism is popular but the ordering of oxygen and ice is still disputed

claims.statement: Coiled carbon ribbons in 2.1-billion-year-old Michigan iron formation are read as the oldest large eukaryotic algae.
claims.asserted_by: Han & Runnegar 1992, Science

status_timeline.source: Han & Runnegar 1992, Science 257:232 — Grypania spiralis from the Negaunee Iron-Formation, Empire Mine, 700–1000 Myr older than any prior site
Marquette Range geochronology, early 2000s — deliberately vague; U–Pb ages on the Marquette Range Supergroup put the Negaunee nearer 1.87 Ga, not 2.1 Ga
Proterozoic palaeobiology debate, 2000s — Grypania's eukaryotic affinity rests on size alone; a giant bacterium is not excluded

claims.statement: Bangiomorpha, a 1.2-billion-year-old red alga from Arctic Canada, is the oldest fossil assignable to a living group.
claims.asserted_by: Butterfield 2000, Paleobiology

status_timeline.source: Butterfield 2000, Paleobiology 26:386 — Bangiomorpha pubescens from the Hunting Formation; also the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction
Proterozoic palaeobiology consensus, 2010s — the red-algal assignment is widely accepted and Bangiomorpha becomes the standard oldest crown-group eukaryote

claims.statement: Rhenium-osmium dating of the host succession moves Bangiomorpha 150 Myr younger, to about 1.047 billion years.
claims.asserted_by: Gibson et al. 2018, Geology

status_timeline.source: Gibson et al. 2018, Geology 46:135 — Re–Os age of 1047 ± 17 Ma on the Bangiomorpha-bearing Bylot Supergroup; eukaryotic photosynthesis back-calculated to ~1.25 Ga

claims.statement: Mitochondria and plastids are domesticated bacteria that were engulfed and kept, not organelles built from scratch.
claims.asserted_by: Sagan (Margulis) 1967, Journal of Theoretical Biology

status_timeline.source: Sagan (Margulis) 1967, Journal of Theoretical Biology — 'On the origin of mitosing cells', rejected by many journals before publication
cell-biology resistance, 1970s — the idea was treated as fringe for roughly a decade after publication
Gray & Doolittle 1982, Microbiological Reviews 46:1 — 'Has the endosymbiont hypothesis been proven?'; organellar sequence data settle mitochondria and plastids

claims.statement: Palaeomagnetism puts Neoproterozoic glacial deposits at the equator, implying the entire ocean froze over.
claims.asserted_by: Kirschvink 1992, in Schopf & Klein eds., The Proterozoic Biosphere (Cambridge University Press), pp. 51–52

status_timeline.source: Kirschvink 1992, The Proterozoic Biosphere, pp. 51–52 — a two-page chapter that coins the term 'snowball Earth' and is largely ignored for six years
Hoffman, Kaufman, Halverson & Schrag 1998, Science — the idea is amplified into a full hypothesis and immediately attacked
Rooney, Strauss, Brandon & Macdonald 2015, Geology — synchronous long-lived global glaciations confirmed; broad but not universal acceptance

claims.statement: Namibian cap carbonates and a collapse in carbon isotopes record a global freeze ending in an extreme greenhouse.
claims.asserted_by: Hoffman, Kaufman, Halverson & Schrag 1998, Science

status_timeline.source: Hoffman, Kaufman, Halverson & Schrag 1998, Science 281:1342 — 'A Neoproterozoic Snowball Earth'; CO2 rising to ~350x modern ends the freeze
Hyde, Crowley, Baum & Peltier 2000, Nature 405:425 — a 'slushball' with an open tropical ocean fits the models at least as well
Rooney et al. 2015, Geology — Re–Os ages show two long, globally synchronous glaciations, hard to explain without near-total ice

claims.statement: Coupled climate-ice models make equatorial ice with an open tropical sea: a slushball rather than a snowball.
claims.asserted_by: Hyde, Crowley, Baum & Peltier 2000, Nature

status_timeline.source: Hyde, Crowley, Baum & Peltier 2000, Nature — a refuge for photosynthetic life that a hard snowball would have killed
snowball modelling debate, 2000s–2010s — the slushball survives as a minority position; sea-glass and refugia arguments blunt its main advantage

claims.statement: Rhenium-osmium ages run the Cryogenian Sturtian glaciation from 717 to 661 Ma, synchronous across three palaeocontinents.
claims.asserted_by: Rooney, Strauss, Brandon & Macdonald 2015, Geology

status_timeline.source: Rooney, Strauss, Brandon & Macdonald 2015, Geology 43:459 — 'A Cryogenian chronology: two long-lasting synchronous Neoproterozoic glaciations'
Cryogenian geochronology consensus, ~2020 — a 56-Myr Sturtian and a short Marinoan ending at 635 Ma are now standard

claims.statement: The freeze-thaw shock and the oxygen pulse that followed set the stage for the first large soft-bodied organisms.
claims.asserted_by: Hoffman, Kaufman, Halverson & Schrag 1998, Science

status_timeline.source: Hoffman et al. 1998, Science — repeated global bottlenecks and post-glacial recovery framed as an evolutionary filter
Neoproterozoic oxygenation debate, 2010s — the correlation is strong but the causal arrow between ice, oxygen and animals is still argued

claims.statement: Disc-shaped impressions in Flinders Ranges sandstone, described in 1947 as jellyfish, were the first Ediacarans found.
claims.asserted_by: Sprigg 1947, Transactions of the Royal Society of South Australia

status_timeline.source: Sprigg 1947, Trans. Roy. Soc. South Australia 71:212 — 'Early Cambrian (?) jellyfishes'; the age was wrong and the paper was largely ignored
Glaessner and Wade, Adelaide, late 1950s — the fauna is recognised as genuinely Precambrian and becomes internationally known

claims.statement: The Ediacara fossils are Precambrian, not Cambrian: complex soft-bodied life predates the Cambrian explosion.
claims.asserted_by: Glaessner and colleagues, University of Adelaide, late 1950s (deliberately vague: the reassignment accrued over several papers)

status_timeline.source: Glaessner, Adelaide, 1959 — Ediacara fauna reassigned below the Cambrian; exact single citation deliberately not pinned
stratigraphic consensus, 1980s — a global Ediacaran assemblage is documented on five continents

claims.statement: The Ediacarans may be a failed experiment: quilted organisms unrelated to any animal phylum that survived.
claims.asserted_by: Seilacher 1992, Journal of the Geological Society (London)

status_timeline.source: Seilacher 1992, J. Geol. Soc. London 149:607 — 'Vendobionta and Psammocorallia: lost constructions of Precambrian evolution'
Ediacaran affinity debate, ~2000 — rival readings place them as lichens, fungi, giant protists, or stem animals
Bobrovskiy et al. 2018, Science — cholesteroids show at least Dickinsonia was an animal, dissolving the strongest version of Vendobionta

claims.statement: Cholesterol biomarkers preserved in Dickinsonia show it was an animal, not a lichen, fungus or failed experiment.
claims.asserted_by: Bobrovskiy, Hope, Ivantsov, Nettersheim, Hallmann & Brocks 2018, Science

status_timeline.source: Bobrovskiy et al. 2018, Science — cholesteroids extracted from Dickinsonia films at Zimnie Gory on the White Sea Winter Coast
Ediacaran palaeobiology, early 2020s — the animal affinity of Dickinsonia is now the majority position

claims.statement: In 2004 the Ediacaran became the first new geological period ratified in over a century, its base fixed at 635 Ma.
claims.asserted_by: International Commission on Stratigraphy 2004 — ratification of the Ediacaran System

status_timeline.source: ICS 2004 — the golden spike is placed at the base of the Nuccaleena cap carbonate at Enorama Creek, Flinders Ranges; the top was then the 542 Ma Cambrian base
Knoll, Walter, Narbonne & Christie-Blick 2006, Lethaia 39:13 — 'The Ediacaran Period: a new addition to the geologic time scale'

claims.statement: Almost every living animal phylum shows up in the fossil record within a geologic eyeblink, with no obvious ancestors below.
claims.asserted_by: Darwin 1859, On the Origin of Species

status_timeline.source: Darwin 1859, On the Origin of Species — flagged the abrupt Cambrian appearance as a serious objection to his own theory
Walcott 1911, Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections 57(5) — described the Burgess Shale fauna found in 1909, deepening rather than dissolving the puzzle
Erwin et al. 2011, Science 334:1091 — molecular clocks plus fossils framed the radiation as fast but not instantaneous

claims.statement: Zircon dating of Siberian sections puts the Cambrian base near 544 Ma and squeezes the main radiation into roughly 10 million years.
claims.asserted_by: Bowring et al. 1993, Science

status_timeline.source: Bowring et al. 1993, Science 261:1293 — U-Pb ash dates from the Siberian Platform put the base near 544 Ma and the Tommotian-Atdabanian at 5-10 Myr
Gradstein et al. 2004, A Geologic Time Scale 2004 — base of the Cambrian revised younger to 542.0 +/- 1.0 Ma as new ash dates accumulated

claims.statement: The Cambrian begins 538.8 million years ago, over five million years later than the 1993 zircon calibration claimed.
claims.asserted_by: Linnemann et al. 2019, Terra Nova

status_timeline.source: Linnemann et al. 2019, Terra Nova 31:49 — CA-ID-TIMS ash-bed ages in Namibia bracketed the Ediacaran-Cambrian transition to 538.99-538.58 Ma
ICS 2023, International Chronostratigraphic Chart — 538.8 Ma adopted for the Cambrian base, defined at the GSSP at Fortune Head, Newfoundland

claims.statement: Ash beds along the Orange River calibrate the Ediacaran-to-Cambrian turnover between 539.6 and 538.0 million years ago.
claims.asserted_by: Nelson et al. 2022, Earth and Planetary Science Letters

status_timeline.source: Nelson et al. 2022, EPSL 580:117396 — six U-Pb dated ash beds on the Neint Nababeep Plateau, northwestern South Africa, span 539.63 to 537.95 Ma
Ediacaran-Cambrian correlation debate of the 2020s — tying regional radiometric records to the trace-fossil-defined GSSP is unresolved; adoption date approximate

claims.statement: Detrital zircons cap the Chengjiang fossil beds at 518.0 million years, fixing the radiation's showpiece deposit in absolute time.
claims.asserted_by: Yang et al. 2018, Journal of the Geological Society

status_timeline.source: Yang et al. 2018, J. Geol. Soc. 175:659 — CA-ID-TIMS on detrital zircons gave a maximum age of 518.03 +/- 0.69 Ma for the Maotianshan Shale, implying a protracted (>22 Myr) explosion
Cambrian geochronology practice since about 2020 — the 518 Ma tie-point is now routinely cited; adoption date approximate

claims.statement: Some Burgess Shale animals are so strange that they may not fit inside any surviving phylum at all.
claims.asserted_by: Whittington 1975, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B

status_timeline.source: Whittington 1975, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 271:1 — redescription of Opabinia regalis found no home for it among living groups
Gould 1989, Wonderful Life — popularised maximal Cambrian disparity and drew immediate pushback
Conway Morris 1998, The Crucible of Creation — argued most oddballs are stem members of known phyla
Phylogenetic consensus of the 2010s — cladistic restudies placed Opabinia and Hallucigenia on the stems of living groups; date approximate

claims.statement: Two thumb-sized jawless fish from Chengjiang carry gill pouches and a notochord, making them the oldest known vertebrates.
claims.asserted_by: Shu et al. 1999, Nature

status_timeline.source: Shu et al. 1999, Nature 402:42 — Myllokunmingia and Haikouichthys described as Early Cambrian craniates

claims.statement: Between roughly 1760 and 1840 Britain moved from muscle and water to coal-fired steam, and never went back.
claims.asserted_by: Toynbee 1884, Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England (published posthumously)

status_timeline.source: Toynbee 1884 — names and periodises the Industrial Revolution as 1760-1840
the periodisation becomes standard in economic history; date approximate
Crafts 1985, British Economic Growth during the Industrial Revolution (Clarendon Press / Oxford) — growth was slower and more gradual than the label implies

claims.statement: Tambora erupted on 10 April 1815, the largest eruption in recorded history, and lost 1,400 metres of its own summit.
claims.asserted_by: Raffles 1817, The History of Java (eyewitness accounts collected from Java); quantified by Stothers 1984, Science 224:1191

status_timeline.source: Raffles 1817 — contemporary eyewitness reports gathered in Java fix the date and scale
Stothers 1984, Science 224:1191 — The Great Tambora Eruption in 1815 and Its Aftermath quantifies the eruption and its atmospheric effects

claims.statement: 1816 had no summer in New England and Europe: June snow, failed harvests, and the West's last great subsistence crisis.
claims.asserted_by: Stommel & Stommel 1979, Scientific American 240(6):176 — The Year Without a Summer

status_timeline.source: Stommel & Stommel 1979 — reconstructs the 1816 cold anomaly from diaries and harvest records
the anomaly is confirmed by instrumental and proxy climate reconstructions; diffuse, no single paper

claims.statement: Tambora's sulfate veil dimmed the northern hemisphere by roughly half a degree, causing the 1816 crop failures.
claims.asserted_by: Humphreys 1913, Journal of the Franklin Institute; synthesised by Oppenheimer 2003, Progress in Physical Geography

status_timeline.source: Humphreys 1913 — volcanic dust in the upper atmosphere proposed as a cause of historical cold years
ice-core sulfate spikes tie the 1816 anomaly to the 1815 eruption; date approximate
Oppenheimer 2003, Progress in Physical Geography — synthesises the forcing, the cooling and the human toll

claims.statement: At 05:29 on 16 July 1945 a plutonium device fired in the New Mexico desert and fused the sand into green glass.
claims.asserted_by: Manhattan Project records, declassified 1945 (Smyth Report, Atomic Energy for Military Purposes)

status_timeline.source: Smyth Report 1945 — the test is public record within weeks; trinitite is its physical trace

claims.statement: Fallout plutonium and carbon-14 from 1950s bomb tests are a sharp, global, permanent layer in the world's sediments.
claims.asserted_by: Waters et al. 2015, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists 71(3):46 — Can nuclear weapons fallout mark the beginning of the Anthropocene epoch?

status_timeline.source: Waters et al. 2015 — the bomb spike put forward as the sharpest available global stratigraphic marker
the marker's reality is not disputed even by those who reject the epoch

claims.statement: Humanity has become a geological force, and the epoch we live in should be renamed the Anthropocene.
claims.asserted_by: Crutzen & Stoermer 2000, IGBP Newsletter 41

status_timeline.source: Crutzen & Stoermer 2000, IGBP Newsletter — the term coined, with an informal 1800 CE start
Crutzen 2002, Nature — 'Geology of mankind' brings the term to a general scientific audience
the ICS convenes an Anthropocene Working Group to test the concept formally
rejected as a formal epoch but retained in wide informal use across the earth and social sciences

claims.statement: The Anthropocene should begin in 1952, with a golden spike in the varved mud of Crawford Lake, Ontario.
claims.asserted_by: McCarthy et al. 2023, The Anthropocene Review — the varved succession of Crawford Lake, Milton, Ontario as a candidate GSSP

status_timeline.source: AWG names Crawford Lake the GSSP candidate in July 2023; the horizon voted to the 1952 varve on the 239+240Pu rise; formal proposal submitted 31 October 2023
4 March 2024 — the ICS Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy votes it down, 12 of 18 against

claims.statement: The 2024 vote that killed the Anthropocene was itself attacked as procedurally irregular before being upheld.
claims.asserted_by: public commentary following the March 2024 SQS vote, including Oreskes' 'sham' remark; IUGS and the ICS subcommission chairs subsequently affirmed the process

status_timeline.source: AWG members and outside historians allege irregularities — Oreskes calls the vote 'a sham'; the IUGS statement of 20 March 2024 confirms the vote followed its statutes, and the subcommission chairs back the ICS Executive near-unanimously

claims.statement: Human interference with climate began 8,000 years ago with forest clearance and rice paddies, not in 1952.
claims.asserted_by: Ruddiman 2003, Climatic Change — The anthropogenic greenhouse era began thousands of years ago

status_timeline.source: Ruddiman 2003 — anomalous Holocene CO2 and CH4 attributed to early farming
critics argue the early emissions are far too small; the hypothesis remains a live minority position

claims.statement: Burning fossil carbon at industrial scale is what made humans a planetary force, so the Anthropocene starts around 1800.
claims.asserted_by: Steffen, Crutzen & McNeill 2007, Ambio — The Anthropocene: Are Humans Now Overwhelming the Great Forces of Nature?

status_timeline.source: Steffen et al. 2007, Ambio — Stage 1 of the Anthropocene dated to the industrial era
the AWG shifts to a 1950s 'Great Acceleration' start with a sharper stratigraphic signal
with no formal epoch, the industrial start date survives as one informal usage among several

claims.statement: Rock layers were laid down in sequence, the lowest first, so strata record an order of events.
claims.asserted_by: Steno 1669, De solido intra solidum naturaliter contento prodromus

status_timeline.source: Steno 1669, Florence — superposition, original horizontality and lateral continuity, from dissecting Tuscan hillsides
stratigraphic practice, c. 1800 — superposition becomes the working assumption of field geology

claims.statement: The rock cycle has run so long that the record shows no vestige of a beginning and no prospect of an end.
claims.asserted_by: Hutton 1788, Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh

status_timeline.source: Hutton 1788 — the angular unconformity at Siccar Point read as two complete cycles of deposition, uplift and erosion
scriptural geology, c. 1800 — an indefinitely old Earth is resisted on theological grounds
geological consensus, c. 1840 — an Earth vastly older than human record is taken as established

claims.statement: Present-day rates of erosion and deposition are enough to explain the past; no former catastrophes need be invoked.
claims.asserted_by: Lyell 1830-1833, Principles of Geology (John Murray)

status_timeline.source: Lyell 1830-1833 — Hutton's deep time restated as strict uniformity of rate as well as of process
geological consensus, c. 1860 — uniformitarianism becomes the disciplinary default
Alvarez et al. 1980, Science — a sudden extraterrestrial catastrophe reopens the question of rate

claims.statement: The Earth's heat loss limits its age to somewhere between twenty and four hundred million years, most likely about a hundred.
claims.asserted_by: Thomson (Kelvin) 1862, Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh

status_timeline.source: Thomson 1862, On the Secular Cooling of the Earth — a cooling sphere with no internal heat source
physical consensus, 1870s-1890s — Kelvin's authority compresses the geological timescale against the objections of geologists and of Darwin
Curie & Laborde 1903, Comptes Rendus — radium generates heat, so the Earth is not a simply cooling body
Holmes 1913, The Age of the Earth — radiometric ages exceed Kelvin's ceiling outright

claims.statement: Lead accumulating in uranium minerals gives rock ages from four hundred million up to two thousand million years.
claims.asserted_by: Boltwood 1907, American Journal of Science

status_timeline.source: Boltwood 1907 — the first uranium-lead ages, on ten mineral samples
age-of-the-Earth debate, 1920s — radiometric ages accepted in principle, the numbers still moving
Patterson 1956 — the meteoritic lead isochron settles the figure near 4.55 Ga

claims.statement: Radioactive decay makes the Earth at least sixteen hundred million years old, far beyond any cooling estimate.
claims.asserted_by: Holmes 1913, The Age of the Earth (Harper & Brothers)

status_timeline.source: Holmes 1913 — the first sustained argument for a radiometric geological timescale
National Research Council report on the age of the Earth, 1931 — radiometric dating formally endorsed
Patterson 1956 — superseded by the meteoritic lead isochron

claims.statement: Matching Carboniferous floras and glacial beds on now-separate continents mean the landmasses were once joined.
claims.asserted_by: Wegener 1915, Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane

status_timeline.source: Wegener 1915 — Pangaea argued from the fit of coastlines and the distribution of the Glossopteris flora
American Association of Petroleum Geologists symposium, 1926-1928 — drift rejected, largely for lacking a mechanism
Vine & Matthews 1963, Nature — magnetic striping on the seafloor supplies the missing mechanism
Morgan 1968 and Le Pichon 1968 — plate tectonics becomes the framework of the earth sciences

claims.statement: The Cretaceous-Tertiary boundary sits at sixty-five million years, the round figure carried by textbooks for decades.
claims.asserted_by: Cretaceous-Tertiary boundary age, textbook consensus c. 1980-2005 (no single originating paper)

status_timeline.source: timescale consensus, 1980s-1990s — deliberately vague attribution; 65 Ma was a rounded figure in general circulation, not one group's result
Renne et al. 2013, Science — recalibration moves the boundary to 66.043 Ma and the round number retires

claims.statement: Argon dating of boundary tektites and ash puts the extinction at 66.043 million years, to within eleven thousand.
claims.asserted_by: Renne et al. 2013, Science

status_timeline.source: Renne et al. 2013, Science — Time Scales of Critical Events Around the Cretaceous-Paleogene Boundary
geochronological consensus, mid-2010s — 66.0 Ma adopted by the international timescale

claims.statement: The second great freeze, the Marinoan, ends at 635 million years, the boundary that now opens the Ediacaran.
claims.asserted_by: Condon et al. 2005, Science

status_timeline.source: Condon et al. 2005, Science — U-Pb ages from the Doushantuo Formation, South China
chronostratigraphic consensus — 635 Ma ratified as the base of the Ediacaran, at the top of the Marinoan cap carbonate

claims.statement: Aeromagnetic and gravity survey reveals a buried circular structure about 180 km across beneath northern Yucatan.
claims.asserted_by: Penfield & Camargo Z. 1981, Society of Exploration Geophysicists 51st Annual International Meeting, Technical Program Abstracts, p. 37

status_timeline.source: Penfield & Camargo Z. 1981, SEG 51st Annual Meeting abstracts p. 37, 'Definition of a major igneous zone in the central Yucatan platform with aeromagnetics and gravity' - read as a buried igneous zone, with no age; the Pemex well data behind it stayed unpublished
Hildebrand et al. 1991, Geology 19:867 - the same anomaly reinterpreted as an impact crater and confirmed by shocked quartz in the well cores

claims.statement: Shocked quartz and impact melt in Yucatan well cores identify the 180 km structure as the Cretaceous/Tertiary impact crater.
claims.asserted_by: Hildebrand, Penfield, Kring, Pilkington, Camargo Z., Jacobsen & Boynton 1991, Geology

status_timeline.source: Hildebrand et al. 1991, Geology 19:867 - the crater the Alvarez hypothesis had been missing for eleven years; age stated only as 'a K/T boundary age is indicated'
Schulte et al. 2010, Science 327:1214 - a 41-author review treats the Chicxulub identification as settled
Morgan et al. 2016, Science 354:878 - IODP-ICDP Expedition 364 drills the offshore peak ring and recovers uplifted granite

claims.statement: Argon dating gives 65.0 Ma for Chicxulub melt rock and for Haitian boundary tektites, showing them to be one event.
claims.asserted_by: Swisher et al. 1992, Science

status_timeline.source: Swisher et al. 1992, Science 257:954-958 - coeval 40Ar/39Ar ages of 65.0 Ma from crater melt rock and from Cretaceous-Tertiary boundary tektites
impact geochronology consensus through the late 1990s - 65.0 Ma becomes the textbook figure for the impact and the boundary alike
Renne et al. 2013, Science 339:684 - recalibrated argon monitor standards move the same rocks about 1 Myr older, to 66.04 Ma

claims.statement: Recalibrated argon dating puts the impact at 66.043 Ma, synchronous with the boundary to within 32,000 years.
claims.asserted_by: Renne, Deino, Hilgen, Kuiper, Mark, Mitchell, Morgan, Mundil & Smit 2013, Science

status_timeline.source: Renne et al. 2013, Science 339:684-687 - impact glass at 66.038 +/- 0.049 Ma and the boundary at 66.043 +/- 0.011 Ma, indistinguishable
geochronological consensus since about 2016 - 66.04 Ma is carried into the International Chronostratigraphic Chart and unchallenged by later work

claims.statement: Core Yaxcopoil-1 is read as showing the impact struck about 300,000 years before the boundary, so it did not cause it.
claims.asserted_by: Keller, Adatte, Stinnesbeck, Rebolledo-Vieyra, Urrutia Fucugauchi, Kramar & Stueben 2004, PNAS

status_timeline.source: Keller et al. 2004, PNAS 101:3753-3758 - five independent proxies in the crater's own core (sedimentology, biostratigraphy, magnetostratigraphy, stable isotopes, iridium) are read as placing the impact about 300 kyr below the boundary
Schulte et al. 2010, Science 327:1214 - the review panel rejects the Yaxcopoil-1 stratigraphy as reworked crater fill
Renne et al. 2013, Science 339:684 - argon dating finds impact and boundary synchronous within 32 kyr; the pre-boundary reading survives only as a minority position

claims.statement: Drilling the offshore peak ring recovers granite uplifted from 10 km depth, confirming dynamic collapse of the crater.
claims.asserted_by: Morgan et al. 2016, Science

status_timeline.source: Morgan et al. 2016, Science 354:878-882 - Expedition 364 core M0077A shows the peak ring is uplifted, shocked basement, favouring the dynamic collapse model
peak-ring formation consensus since about 2020 - reproduced across subsequent IODP-ICDP Expedition 364 syntheses

claims.statement: A worldwide iridium spike in the boundary clay implies a 10 km asteroid struck Earth and darkened the sky.
claims.asserted_by: Alvarez, Alvarez, Asaro & Michel 1980, Science

status_timeline.source: Alvarez et al. 1980, Science 208:1095-1108 - iridium 30x background in the Bottaccione Gorge at Gubbio, and in Denmark and New Zealand

volcanist critique through the 1980s, led by C.B. Officer and later G. Keller - the iridium read as mantle-derived and the extinction as gradual; no crater was known. Diffuse rather than one paper, so deliberately unpinned
Hildebrand et al. 1991, Geology 19:867 - the missing crater is identified at Chicxulub and the impact reading becomes majority opinion
Schulte et al. 2010, Science 327:1214 - a 41-author review affirms impact as the trigger

claims.statement: The 2004 geologic time scale places the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary at 65.5 million years.
claims.asserted_by: Gradstein, Ogg & Smith (eds.) 2004, A Geologic Time Scale 2004 (Cambridge University Press)

status_timeline.source: Gradstein, Ogg & Smith (eds.) 2004, A Geologic Time Scale 2004 - the base of the Danian is set at 65.5 Ma, and 65.5 +/- 0.3 Ma is the ratified figure for most of the 2000s
Gradstein et al. (eds.) 2012, The Geologic Time Scale 2012, following Kuiper et al. 2008, Science 320:500 and Renne et al. 2011, GCA 75:5097 - argon recalibration moves the boundary to 66.0 Ma

claims.statement: Argon dating and astrochronology fix the boundary at 66.043 Ma, with the extinction inside 32,000 years of it.
claims.asserted_by: Renne, Deino, Hilgen, Kuiper, Mark, Mitchell, Morgan, Mundil & Smit 2013, Science

status_timeline.source: Renne et al. 2013, Science 339:684-687 - the boundary at 66.043 +/- 0.011 Ma, ending three decades of a nominal 65 Ma
chronostratigraphic consensus since about 2016 - 66.0 Ma adopted on the International Chronostratigraphic Chart

claims.statement: Deccan flood volcanism, not an impact, is proposed as the principal driver of the end-Cretaceous extinction.
claims.asserted_by: Courtillot, Besse, Vandamme, Montigny, Jaeger & Cappetta 1986, Earth and Planetary Science Letters

status_timeline.source: Courtillot et al. 1986, EPSL 80:361-374, 'Deccan flood basalts at the Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary?' - a flood basalt of the right size at the right moment is offered as an alternative to the asteroid
Hildebrand et al. 1991, Geology 19:867 - the discovery of the Chicxulub crater pushes volcanism to a secondary role

Courtillot & Fluteau 2010, Science 328:973-974, 'Cretaceous Extinctions: The Volcanic Hypothesis' - a technical comment rejecting Schulte et al.'s dismissal of volcanism; the hypothesis survives as a contributory cause

claims.statement: A 41-author review concludes the Chicxulub impact alone triggered the mass extinction at the boundary.
claims.asserted_by: Schulte et al. 2010, Science

status_timeline.source: Schulte et al. 2010, Science 327:1214-1218 - a deliberately consensus-forming review across 41 authors and twelve countries

Archibald, Clemens, Padian et al. 2010, Science 328:973 ('Cretaceous Extinctions: Multiple Causes') and Courtillot & Fluteau 2010, Science 328:973-974 ('Cretaceous Extinctions: The Volcanic Hypothesis') - two technical comments in the same issue reject the single-cause conclusion
impact-primacy consensus through the 2010s - most workers accept impact as trigger while allowing Deccan volcanism as a stressor

claims.statement: Pre-1991 time scales place the Permian-Triassic boundary near 245 million years.
claims.asserted_by: pre-1991 geologic time-scale consensus, 1980s - no single verified originating table

status_timeline.source: pre-1991 geologic time-scale consensus - about 245 Ma, interpolated from sparse mineral ages with no direct date on the boundary itself. Attribution deliberately left vague: the figure is usually traced to the Cambridge scales of Harland and colleagues, but I could not confirm whether the 1982 edition or the 1989 edition (published 1990) is the one carrying 245.0 Ma, and the 1982 scale is often cited nearer 248 Ma
Claoue-Long et al. 1991, EPSL 105:182-190 - the first direct age on the boundary clay comes out about 6 Myr older
Bowring et al. 1998, Science 280:1039 - high-precision U-Pb settles the boundary near 251 Ma and the 245 Ma figure is abandoned

claims.statement: Ion-probe zircon dating of the Meishan boundary clay gives the first direct age, 251.2 million years.
claims.asserted_by: Claoue-Long, Zhang Zichao, Ma Guogan & Du Shaohua 1991, Earth and Planetary Science Letters

status_timeline.source: Claoue-Long et al. 1991, EPSL 105:182-190 - SHRIMP zircon age of 251.2 +/- 3.4 Ma (2 sigma) on the bentonite boundary clay in the Chinese stratotype
Bowring et al. 1998, Science 280:1039 - isotope-dilution U-Pb on the same sections is ten times more precise

claims.statement: High-precision uranium-lead zircon ages put the boundary at 251.4 Ma and the main kill inside a million years.
claims.asserted_by: Bowring, Erwin, Jin, Martin, Davidek & Wang 1998, Science

status_timeline.source: Bowring et al. 1998, Science 280:1039-1045 - 251.4 +/- 0.3 Ma from south China, with the loss of ~85% of marine species in under 1 Myr
end-Permian geochronology consensus through the early 2000s - 251 Ma becomes the standard figure
Shen et al. 2011, Science 334:1367 - CA-ID-TIMS on the same beds moves the onset to 252.28 Ma

claims.statement: Chemically abraded zircon ages move the extinction onset to 252.28 Ma and compress it to under 200,000 years.
claims.asserted_by: Shen, Crowley, Wang, Bowring, Erwin, Sadler et al. 2011, Science

status_timeline.source: Shen et al. 2011, Science 334:1367-1372, 'Calibrating the End-Permian Mass Extinction' - onset at 252.28 +/- 0.08 Ma
Burgess, Bowring & Shen 2014, PNAS 111:3316 - revised tracer calibration and new beds move the same event to 251.94 Ma

claims.statement: The extinction runs from 251.941 to 251.880 million years, an interval of only about 60,000 years.
claims.asserted_by: Burgess, Bowring & Shen 2014, PNAS

status_timeline.source: Burgess, Bowring & Shen 2014, PNAS 111:3316-3321 - 251.941 +/- 0.037 to 251.880 +/- 0.031 Ma, a duration of 60 +/- 48 kyr (restated as 61 +/- 48 ky in Burgess & Bowring 2015)
end-Permian geochronology consensus since the late 2010s - 251.9 Ma is carried onto the International Chronostratigraphic Chart

claims.statement: Siberian Traps magmatism began roughly 300,000 years before the extinction and is its most likely trigger.
claims.asserted_by: Burgess & Bowring 2015, Science Advances

status_timeline.source: Burgess & Bowring 2015, Science Advances 1:e1500470 - about two-thirds of the lava and pyroclastic volume erupted over ~300 kyr before and concurrent with the extinction, and the balance continued at least 500 kyr after it ended
mass extinction causation consensus since about 2020 - the Siberian Traps trigger is standard, with the exact kill mechanism still argued

claims.statement: Laser argon dating shows the Siberian flood basalts erupted in well under a million years, around 248 Ma.
claims.asserted_by: Renne & Basu 1991, Science

status_timeline.source: Renne & Basu 1991, Science 253:176-179 - 40Ar/39Ar laser-heating gives eruption over 900,000 +/- 800,000 years beginning at about 248 Ma; the brevity is the finding, the absolute age is not
Kamo et al. 2003, EPSL 214:75 - U-Pb on zircon and baddeleyite puts the same rocks about 4 Myr older, at 251.7 Ma

claims.statement: Uranium-lead ages on zircon and baddeleyite put the main Siberian eruption at 251.7 Ma, inside one million years.
claims.asserted_by: Kamo, Czamanske, Amelin, Fedorenko, Davis & Trofimov 2003, Earth and Planetary Science Letters

status_timeline.source: Kamo et al. 2003, EPSL 214:75-91 - rapid eruption at 251.7 +/- 0.4 Ma, coincident with the Permian-Triassic boundary as then dated
Burgess & Bowring 2015, Science Advances 1:e1500470 - the province is shown to run from 252.24 to 251.4 Ma, longer and older than a single 251.7 Ma pulse

claims.statement: Zircon and perovskite ages run Siberian magmatism from 252.24 to 251.4 Ma, straddling the extinction.
claims.asserted_by: Burgess & Bowring 2015, Science Advances

status_timeline.source: Burgess & Bowring 2015, Science Advances 1:e1500470 - voluminous magmatism before, during and after the extinction, with sills emplaced concomitant with the extinction and continuing at least 500 kyr into the Triassic
large igneous province geochronology consensus since about 2020 - the 252.24-251.4 Ma window is the standard frame

claims.statement: Millions of cubic kilometres of lava and sill buried the Siberian craton, the largest known continental flood basalt.
claims.asserted_by: Siberian Traps volumetric consensus, 1990s-2010s, as summarised in Burgess & Bowring 2015, Science Advances

status_timeline.source: Burgess & Bowring 2015, Science Advances 1:e1500470, summarising two decades of mapping and drilling - no serious dispute about the province's existence or its scale, only its tempo

claims.statement: Palaeomagnetism and argon ages compress the main Deccan eruption to under a million years at the boundary.
claims.asserted_by: Courtillot, Besse, Vandamme, Montigny, Jaeger & Cappetta 1986, Earth and Planetary Science Letters

status_timeline.source: Courtillot et al. 1986, EPSL 80:361-374 - three magnetic polarity intervals imply well under 1 Myr of eruption spanning the boundary
flood-basalt geochronology through the late 1980s and 1990s repeatedly confirms a short, boundary-straddling eruption
Schoene et al. 2019 and Sprain et al. 2019, Science 363:862 and 866 - two high-precision chronologies published together disagree on how the volume splits across the boundary

claims.statement: Uranium-lead ages resolve four eruptive pulses between 66.3 and 65.5 Ma, the first beginning before the impact.
claims.asserted_by: Schoene, Eddy, Samperton, Keller, Keller, Adatte & Khadri 2019, Science

status_timeline.source: Schoene et al. 2019, Science 363:862-866 - four high-volume events each lasting under 100 kyr, at ~66.3-66.15, ~66.1-66.0, ~65.9-65.8 and ~65.6-65.5 Ma; the first preceded the Chicxulub impact and the Poladpur pulse began tens of thousands of years before the extinction at ~90% probability
Sprain et al. 2019, Science 363:866-870 - published in the same issue, the argon chronology finds no such discrete pulses

claims.statement: Argon dating says over three-quarters of Deccan lava erupted after the boundary, too late to have done the killing.
claims.asserted_by: Sprain, Renne, Vanderkluysen, Pande, Self & Mittal 2019, Science

status_timeline.source: Sprain et al. 2019, Science 363:866-870 - the Deccan did not erupt in three discrete pulses; over 90% of the volume erupted in under 1 Myr, with about 75% of it emplaced after the boundary
Schoene et al. 2019, Science 363:862 - the U-Pb chronology resolves discrete pulses and places more of the volume before the boundary; the two methods remain unreconciled

claims.statement: Seismic energy from Chicxulub may have shifted Deccan plumbing into a higher-output state within 50,000 years.
claims.asserted_by: Renne, Sprain, Richards, Self, Vanderkluysen & Pande 2015, Science

status_timeline.source: Renne et al. 2015, Science 350:76-78 - an impact-induced state shift inferred from a coincidence of timing rather than a demonstrated mechanism
Schoene et al. 2019, Science 363:862 - the U-Pb pulses do not line up with the impact, weakening the trigger claim

claims.statement: Banded iron formations and the first red beds are read as recording oxygen rising near two billion years ago.
claims.asserted_by: Cloud 1972, American Journal of Science

status_timeline.source: Cloud 1972, American Journal of Science 272:537-548, 'A working model of the primitive Earth' - oxygen from cyanobacteria titrated first by dissolved iron
Precambrian atmosphere consensus through the 1980s - the oxygen rise pinned loosely by iron-formation and red-bed stratigraphy, with no sharp date
Farquhar, Bao & Thiemens 2000, Science 289:756 - a sharper sulfur-isotope proxy moves the transition several hundred million years older

claims.statement: Sulfur isotope anomalies end after 2.45 Ga, placing the loss of the anoxic atmosphere between 2.45 and 2.09 Ga.
claims.asserted_by: Farquhar, Bao & Thiemens 2000, Science

status_timeline.source: Farquhar, Bao & Thiemens 2000, Science 289:756-758 - anomalous 33S requires ultraviolet photolysis of SO2 in an ozone-free atmosphere; the paper states the sulfur cycle changed 'between 2090 and 2450 million years ago', with strong anomalies confined to before 2450 Ma
Bekker et al. 2004, Nature 427:117 - South African and Canadian sections independently narrow the same transition, and the S-MIF proxy becomes standard
Luo et al. 2016, Science Advances 2:e1600134 - continuous drill core puts the disappearance at 2.33 Ga, near the young end of Farquhar's bracket

claims.statement: South African and Canadian sections bracket the rise of atmospheric oxygen between 2.32 and 2.22 billion years.
claims.asserted_by: Bekker, Holland, Wang, Rumble, Stein, Hannah, Coetzee & Beukes 2004, Nature

status_timeline.source: Bekker et al. 2004, Nature 427:117-120, 'Dating the rise of atmospheric oxygen' - the rise had occurred between 2.32 and 2.22 Ga; coordinates are the Transvaal Supergroup type area, though the paper also uses Huronian sections in Canada
Luo et al. 2016, Science Advances 2:e1600134 - a continuous core through the same Transvaal succession sharpens the transition to 2.33 Ga, just outside Bekker's older bound

claims.statement: Sulfur isotopes in a continuous South African drill core constrain permanent oxygenation to 2.33 Ga, reached in 1-10 Myr.
claims.asserted_by: Luo, Ono, Beukes, Wang, Xie & Summons 2016, Science Advances

status_timeline.source: Luo et al. 2016, Science Advances 2:e1600134 - three coeval cores through the Rooihoogte-Timeball Hill transition 'precisely constrain the GOE to 2.33 billion years ago', with oxygenation occurring within 1 to 10 Myr; the chronology is anchored on a Re-Os age of 2316 +/- 7 Ma for the formation boundary
Gumsley et al. 2017, PNAS 114:1811 - U-Pb on the Ongeluk lavas dates the onset about 100 Myr earlier, at 2.43 Ga, with oscillations after
Poulton et al. 2021, Nature 592:232 - argues permanent oxygenation waited until 2.22 Ga; the 2.33 Ga figure remains the most used but is not settled

claims.statement: Ongeluk lava ages of 2426 Ma push the onset of oxygenation to 2.43 Ga, with oxygen oscillating for 200 Myr after.
claims.asserted_by: Gumsley, Chamberlain, Bleeker, Soderlund, de Kock, Larsson & Bekker 2017, PNAS

status_timeline.source: Gumsley et al. 2017, PNAS 114:1811-1816, 'Timing and tempo of the Great Oxidation Event' - the Ongeluk large igneous province at ~2426 Ma dates the oldest Paleoproterozoic glaciation and the start of oxygenation
Poulton et al. 2021, Nature 592:232 - agrees oxygen oscillated but sets the permanent transition 200 Myr later than Gumsley's onset

claims.statement: Sulfur isotopes show oxygen oscillating for 200 Myr, with permanent oxygenation only at 2.22 billion years.
claims.asserted_by: Poulton, Bekker, Cumming, Zerkle, Canfield & Johnston 2021, Nature

status_timeline.source: Poulton et al. 2021, Nature 592:232-236, 'A 200-million-year delay in permanent atmospheric oxygenation' - S-MIF returns repeatedly after 2.33 Ga
the 2.33 Ga figure of Luo et al. 2016 remains in wide use; the two chronologies of the Transvaal basin are not reconciled

claims.statement: A shift in volcanic gases from reducing to oxidising is proposed as the cause of the oxygen rise.
claims.asserted_by: Holland 2002, Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta

status_timeline.source: Holland 2002, GCA 66:3811-3826, 'Volcanic gases, black smokers, and the great oxidation event' - a mantle, not biological, trigger

Friedrich et al. 2006 and Manning et al. 2006, Science 312:548 and 565 - both place the eruption before 1600 BCE

Pearson et al. 2018, Science Advances 4:eaar8241 - annual tree-ring calibration lowers the plausible range by up to a century

claims.statement: The giant-planet instability happened shortly after Solar System t0 at 4.567 Ga and within the first hundred million years, long before the Late Heavy Bombardment and before the Earth had finished accreting.

status_timeline.source: Nesvorny, Vokrouhlicky, Bottke & Levison 2018, Nature Astronomy 2:878-882, doi 10.1038/s41550-018-0564-3 - 'Evidence for very early migration of the Solar System planets from the Patroclus-Menoetius binary Jupiter Trojan'; migration 'started shortly after t_0', with 'the disk had to have been dispersed by migrating planets within <100 Myr of t_0' as the upper bound. Liu, Raymond & Jacobson 2022, Nature 604:643-646, doi 10.1038/s41586-022-04535-1 - 'Early Solar System instability triggered by dispersal of the gaseous disk'; an independent dynamical route to an early instability, but tied to gas-disk dispersal 'a few to ten million years after the birth of the Solar System', earlier than the window given here. It is one primary modelling paper proposing one mechanism, not a field survey, so the early instability is the strong default rather than settled consensus.

claims.statement: The composition of the volatiles added to the atmosphere and ocean changed gradually around 2.3 Ga, after which only a fraction of the sulfur gases could still be reduced to pyrite.
claims.asserted_by: Holland 2002, Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta 66(21):3811-3826, doi 10.1016/S0016-7037(02)00950-X

status_timeline.source: Holland 2002, GCA 66(21):3811-3826, doi 10.1016/S0016-7037(02)00950-X, 'Volcanic gases, black smokers, and the great oxidation event' - gradual changes in the composition of volatiles added to the atmosphere-ocean system are held responsible for the G.O.E. ca. 2.3 Ga; before 2.3 Ga all of the sulfur gases could be reduced to pyrite, since 2.3 Ga only a fraction could. Holland says 'gradual changes', not a step.

Li & Lee 2004, EPSL 228:483-493 - V/Sc in Archean basalts back to 3.5 Ga gives source fO2 differing from the modern convecting mantle by no more than 0.3 log units, with little or no secular evolution. The paper is about mantle fO2 and does not engage Holland directly, but it removes the most obvious driver a volatile-composition change would need.

Nicklas, Puchtel, Ash et al. 2019, GCA 250:49-75 - V partitioning in komatiites and picrites recovers approximately 1.3 delta-FMQ log units of oxidation from 3.48 to 1.87 Ga and near-constant fO2 since: a real secular shift, but far slower and more smeared than anything resembling a step at 2.3 Ga (see also Nicklas, Puchtel & Ash 2018, GCA 222:447-466, doi 10.1016/j.gca.2017.11.002)

status_timeline.source: Kump & Barley 2007, Nature 448(7157):1033-1036, doi 10.1038/nature06058 - the predominant Archaean O2 sink, submarine volcanism, was 'abruptly and permanently diminished' at the Archaean-Proterozoic transition; a tectonic rather than a biological trigger for the oxygen rise

status_timeline.source: Berry & Boucot 1973, GSA Bulletin 84:275-284, 'Glacio-eustatic control of Late Ordovician-Early Silurian platform sedimentation and faunal changes'
Brenchley et al. 1994, Geology 22(4):295-298, doi 10.1130/0091-7613(1994)022<0295:BAIEFA>2.3.CO;2 - oxygen and carbon isotope excursions showed a real ice age, not merely a eustatic fall

Finnegan et al. 2011, Science 331(6019):903-906, doi 10.1126/science.1200803 - clumped isotopes find ice present well before and after the Hirnantian, making the short event the glacial maximum rather than the whole glaciation. status_timeline.source: Haq 2014, Global and Planetary Change 113:44-58, doi 10.1016/j.gloplacha.2013.12.007, 'Cretaceous eustasy revisited' - the curve peaks in the earliest Turonian at approximately 240-250 m above present datum, dated 93.5 Ma, and falls as a first-order trend through the Late Cretaceous, with 58 third-order events resolved in the short-term curve

claims.asserted_by: Fladmark 1979, American Antiquity 44(1):55-69, doi 10.2307/279189 - Routes: Alternate Migration Corridors for Early Man in North America. The absolute window here is approximate: the paper argued feasibility, not a date.

status_timeline.source: Fladmark 1979, American Antiquity 44(1):55-69 - palaeoenvironmental and archaeological grounds for coastal refugia; a minority position for two decades

status_timeline.source: Warren & Hankey 1989, Aegean Bronze Age Chronology (Bristol Classical Press, 230 pp., ISBN 0-906515-67-X) - the standard codification of the conventional Egyptian-synchronism chronology of Aegean prehistory, named as the conventional chronology by Manning et al. 2006. status_timeline.source: Retallack 2011, J. Geol. 119(3):235-258, doi 10.1086/659144, 'Woodland Hypothesis for Devonian Tetrapod Evolution' - depth to calcic horizon in northern Appalachian palaeosols as a rainfall proxy; every tetrapod bone, trackway and fossil tree in that region falls in the humid deep-calcic intervals and none in the shallow-calcic aridland soils, argued against Romer's drying-pond escape hypothesis. the aquatic reading of the earliest tetrapods - polydactylous, gill-bearing limbs in Acanthostega and Ichthyostega (Coates & Clack 1990, Nature 347:66-69, doi 10.1038/347066a0, which concludes digited limbs 'may have been adaptations to an aquatic rather than a terrestrial environment') and the synthesis in Clack 2012, Gaining Ground, 2nd edn (Indiana University Press, print ISBN 9780253356758) - remains the majority position; the woodland hypothesis is a minority habitat argument and this date is approximate

claims.statement: Mammals are one twig of the land-vertebrate stem the Devonian tetrapods started: fish to amphibian to amniote to synapsid, an unbroken lineage.

status_timeline.source: Romer 1933, Vertebrate Paleontology, 1st edn (University of Chicago Press) - the reorganisation of the labyrinthodont amphibians and the classification that made the tetrapod-amniote-synapsid-mammal sequence the standard framework. Romer 1966, Vertebrate Paleontology, 3rd edn (University of Chicago Press) - the sequence restated and refined; no rival ancestry for mammals has been seriously advanced

status_timeline.source: Walls 1942, The Vertebrate Eye and Its Adaptive Radiation (Cranbrook Institute of Science, Bulletin 19, Bloomfield Hills, xiv+785 pp.) - comparing reptile, bird and mammal visual systems, Walls argued placental mammals passed through a prolonged nocturnal phase while dinosaurs held the day
